Text: {{c1::Certification::process}} is the exam-based verification that a provider meets {{c2::minimum competency standards}} for emergency care.
Back Extra: Distinguish: certification verifies competency; licensure is the legal authority to practice; credentialing checks qualifications.

Text: {{c1::Licensure::status}} is the {{c2::legal authority to practice}} in your state, granted after certification.
Back Extra: Distinguish: certification verifies you meet the standards; licensure is the state granting legal authority to practice.

Text: {{c1::Credentialing::process}} is the verification of a health care provider's {{c2::qualifications}}, the phase after licensure.
Back Extra: Cue: credentialing can add or limit an EMT's specific skills, beyond the base scope of practice.

Text: The four EMS licensure levels, from least to most training, are {{c1::emergency medical responder (EMR)}}, {{c1::EMT}}, {{c1::advanced EMT (AEMT)}}, and {{c1::paramedic}}.
Back Extra: Cue: scope of practice widens at each level — EMR is the most basic, paramedic the most advanced.

Text: Beyond the EMT level, an AEMT adds selected {{c1::advanced life support (ALS)::level of care}} skills — IV/IO therapy, advanced airway adjuncts, and a few medications.
Back Extra: Distinguish: an AEMT does more than an EMT but less than a paramedic, who has the full ALS scope.

Text: The AEMT course typically runs {{c1::200 to 400::hours}} hours.
Back Extra: Distinguish: more than an EMT course (about 150 to 200 hours), and far less than full paramedic training.

Text: The core work of an EMT on a call follows four steps: {{c1::scene size-up}}, {{c1::patient assessment}}, {{c1::treatment}}, and {{c1::transport}}.
Back Extra: Cue: size up the scene (is it safe?), assess to find life threats, treat, then transport to definitive care.

Text: The six EMS functions on the bars of the Star of Life, in order, are {{c1::detection}}, {{c1::reporting}}, {{c1::response}}, {{c1::on-scene care}}, {{c1::care in transit}}, and {{c1::transfer to definitive care}}.
Back Extra: Cue: they trace a call from spotting the emergency (detection) to hospital handoff (transfer to definitive care).

Text: {{c1::Title I::which title?}} of the Americans with Disabilities Act protects EMTs with disabilities seeking employment, requiring employers to make {{c2::reasonable accommodations}}.
Back Extra: Cue: accommodations let an EMT who can perform the job's functional skills pursue the career despite a disability.

Text: Because licensure is a {{c1::state::level of government}} function, the laws regulating how EMS providers operate are enacted at the {{c1::state}} level.
Back Extra: Cue: the state EMS office controls licensure; the local medical director handles day-to-day oversight.

Text: A medical director can {{c1::limit::limit or expand?}} an EMT's scope of practice but cannot expand it beyond what state law already allows.
Back Extra: Pitfall: adding a skill the state has not approved needs state approval first — not just the medical director's say-so.

Text: Your medical director wants to let you perform a skill your state has not approved. Is that allowed? {{c1::No — expanding scope requires state approval first}}
Back Extra: Why: a medical director can limit an EMT's scope but never expand it beyond state law.

Text: The EMS Agenda 2050 envisions an EMS system that is {{c1::inherently safe and effective}}, {{c1::integrated and seamless}}, {{c1::reliable and prepared}}, {{c1::socially equitable}}, {{c1::sustainable and efficient}}, and {{c1::adaptable and innovative}}.
Back Extra: Cue: six guiding principles — anchor each by one word: safety, integration, reliability, equity, sustainability, adaptability.

Text: A {{c1::medical director::role}} is the physician who {{c2::authorizes a service's EMTs to provide care}}.
Back Extra: Cue: the medical director is the working liaison between the EMTs, hospitals, and the medical community, and is who treatment problems get referred to.

Text: Beyond authorizing care, a medical director {{c1::approves the required continuing education and training}} and {{c1::maintains quality control}} across the service.
Back Extra: Cue: quality oversight runs from the medical director down to each individual EMT's own practice.

Text: {{c1::Standing orders::term}} let an EMT act on a specific complaint {{c2::without contacting medical control first}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: standing orders are pre-authorized (off-line) care; they are part of the written protocols.

Text: {{c1::Online::which?}} (direct) medical control is {{c2::real-time direction by phone or radio during a call}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: off-line control is set up ahead of time (standing orders, protocols); online happens live during the call.

Text: {{c1::Off-line::which?}} (indirect) medical control is {{c2::standing orders, protocols, and training set up in advance}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: online control is live phone or radio direction during a call; off-line is established beforehand.

Text: Mid-call, you radio the hospital for permission to give a treatment right now. Which type of medical control is that? {{c1::Online (direct)::online or off-line?}}
Back Extra: Distinguish: pre-written standing orders you follow without calling = off-line (indirect).

Text: {{c1::Mobile integrated health care (MIH)::model}} delivers health care using {{c2::prehospital resources, within the community}}, rather than at a physician's office or hospital.
Back Extra: Cue: MIH improves access to care at an affordable price, connecting patients with resources like social services.

Text: {{c1::Continuous quality improvement (CQI)::process}} is a quality-management process in which team members at every level keep asking {{c2::'how are we doing, and how can we do better?'}}
Back Extra: Cue: CQI is proactive and ongoing, not a one-time inspection; it relies on a just culture that reports errors without blame.

Text: Medical errors are commonly grouped into three sources: a {{c1::rules-based}}, a {{c1::knowledge-based}}, or a {{c1::skills-based}} failure.
Back Extra: Cue: rules = wrong thing per protocol/permission; knowledge = did not know; skills = could not perform it correctly.

Text: {{c1::Public health::field}} examines the health needs of {{c2::entire populations}}, with the goal of {{c3::preventing health problems}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: public health is proactive and population-level; emergency care is reactive and patient-level.

Text: A {{c1::goiter::condition}} is an abnormally large thyroid gland, caused by too little {{c2::iodine}} in the diet.
Back Extra: Ex: adding iodine to table salt is a classic public-health measure that made goiters rare in the US.

Text: {{c1::Primary::primary or secondary?}} prevention is {{c2::stopping an event from ever happening}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: secondary prevention acts after the event to reduce its effects.
Ex: a vaccine is primary prevention.

Text: {{c1::Secondary::primary or secondary?}} prevention is {{c2::reducing the effects of an event that has already happened}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: primary prevention stops the event entirely.
Ex: seatbelts and helmets are secondary — they reduce injury in a crash.

Text: A {{c1::patient advocate::role}} is an EMT who does everything with {{c2::the patient's best interest in mind}}.
Back Extra: Cue: 'Everything you do needs to be done with the patient in mind' is the guiding principle of EMS.
